meta.ogDescription: Verified: Rilke's fourth letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, Worpswede, 16 July 1903. The familiar English wording is M. D. Herter Norton's 1934 translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually easy to pin down: the sentence sits in the fourth of Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet, headed “Worpswede, near Bremen, July 16th, 1903.” The English wording is M. D. Herter Norton’s translation, published by W. W. Norton in 1934 — Rilke’s own German reads “Leben Sie jetzt die Fragen.”

source.excerpt: Do not now seek the answers, which cannot be given you because you would not be able to live them. And the point is, to live everything. Live the questions now. Perhaps you will then gradually, without noticing it, live along some distant day into the answer.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Rilke page ↗ places the sentence in Letters to a Young Poet, Letter Four (16 July 1903), and prints Rilke’s German beside it. It carries no “Misattributed” or “Disputed” entry for this line.

The M. D. Herter Norton translation carries the wording verbatim; in a scanned Norton printing on the Internet Archive ↗ the fourth letter is headed “Worpswede, near Bremen, July 16th, 1903,” and the copyright page reads “Copyright 1934 by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc. Renewed 1962 by M. D. Herter Norton. Revised edition copyright 1954 by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.”

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the 1934 W. W. Norton first US edition ↗ lists M. D. Herter Norton (1892–1985) as translator and describes the book as a translation of Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.

Wikipedia ↗ records that the ten letters were written to Franz Xaver Kappus, a nineteen-year-old military cadet, and first published in German by Insel Verlag in Leipzig in 1929, three years after Rilke’s death.
source.excerptNote: M. D. Herter Norton’s translation. Rilke’s German, as printed on Wikiquote ↗: “Und es handelt sich darum, alles zu leben. Leben Sie jetzt die Fragen. Vielleicht leben Sie dann allmählich, ohne es zu merken, eines fernen Tages in die Antwort hinein.”

source.rightsNote: Attribution and copyright are separate questions here. Rilke’s German original appeared in Briefe an einen jungen Dichter (Insel Verlag, 1929) and is old enough to be public domain in the United States — but the English sentence people actually quote is a translation, and translations carry their own copyright. This wording is M. D. Herter Norton’s: “Copyright 1934 by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc. Renewed 1962 by M. D. Herter Norton,” with a revised edition copyright of 1954. Quote it briefly with credit; do not treat it as free text.

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Born in Prague in 1875 and dead in Switzerland at fifty-one, Rilke is the poet of Duino Elegies, Sonnets to Orpheus and The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge — a writer whose reputation rests on difficulty, not consolation. The lines everyone knows him for, though, come from ten letters he wrote to a stranger: Franz Xaver Kappus, a nineteen-year-old military cadet who sent him poems and asked whether they were any good. Rilke never answered that question, and answered a much larger one instead.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody else wrote this line, and Quote Investigator has never had to litigate it. The errors here are of a different kind — not the wrong author, but the wrong sentence, and a missing name.

items.why: Wikiquote records a second English rendering of the identical German sentence, credited to Stephen Mitchell, which ends “Perhaps then, someday far in the future, you will gradually, without even noticing it, live your way into the answer” — see the variant on Wikiquote ↗. Both translations are legitimate; a sentence that starts in one and finishes in the other is not.

The English words are M. D. Herter Norton’s, not Rilke’s. Rilke wrote “Leben Sie jetzt die Fragen. Vielleicht leben Sie dann allmählich, ohne es zu merken, eines fernen Tages in die Antwort hinein.” The Internet Archive’s record for the 1934 first US edition names Herter Norton as its translator ↗; the quotation almost never travels with her name attached.

It is prose from a private letter, not verse. The line comes from one of ten letters Rilke sent to Franz Xaver Kappus, a nineteen-year-old military cadet; Kappus assembled and published them in 1929, three years after Rilke’s death — Wikipedia on Letters to a Young Poet ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Rilke really did write it — in German, from Worpswede, on 16 July 1903 — and the English sentence everyone quotes is M. D. Herter Norton’s translation, first published by W. W. Norton in 1934 ↗ and still in copyright.

context.heading: Why a cadet got this letter
lead: Franz Xaver Kappus was nineteen, studying at a military academy, and unsure whether he should be a soldier or a poet. He sent his verses to Rilke, who was then only twenty-seven himself, and asked for a verdict. Rilke declined to give one — he told Kappus that no one outside him could judge, and that the useful work was inward. Ten letters followed. Kappus kept them, and published them in 1929, three years after Rilke’s death, as Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.

The fourth letter was written from Worpswede, an artists’ colony near Bremen, and it opens with Rilke saying he had left Paris about ten days earlier, ill and tired. That is the register the famous sentence belongs to: not a maxim issued from serenity, but advice from a young writer who was himself unwell and unsettled, telling an even younger one that the honest move is to stop demanding answers you are not yet able to inhabit.
detailsBody: Rilke wrote in German. Every English form of this sentence is a translator’s choice, and the two best-known choices diverge in exactly the clause people love most. Norton (1934) ends “live along some distant day into the answer.” Stephen Mitchell’s translation, which Wikiquote prints as a variant, ends “live your way into the answer.”

Both are faithful to eines fernen Tages in die Antwort hinein. Neither is more Rilke than the other. What is not defensible is a hybrid: a quotation is only accurate if it stays inside one translator’s sentence from beginning to end.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote places "And the point is, to live everything. Live the questions now. Perhaps you will then gradually, without noticing it, live along some distant day into the answer" in Letters to a Young Poet, Letter Four (16 July 1903), prints Rilke's German original beside it, and notes a variant translation by Stephen Mitchell ending "live your way into the answer". The page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.

A scanned M. D. Herter Norton translation of Letters to a Young Poet contains the sentence verbatim; the fourth letter is headed "Worpswede, near Bremen, July 16th, 1903", the title page reads "Translation by M. D. Herter Norton", and the copyright page reads "Copyright 1934 by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc. / Renewed 1962 by M. D. Herter Norton / Revised edition copyright 1954 by W. W. Norton & Company, Inc."

The Internet Archive's record for the 1934 W. W. Norton (New York) edition of Letters to a Young Poet names M. D. Herter Norton (Mary Dows), 1892-1985, as translator and Franz Xaver Kappus, 1883-1966, as correspondent, and describes it as a translation of Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.

Letters to a Young Poet collects ten letters Rilke wrote to Franz Xaver Kappus, a nineteen-year-old military cadet, and was first published in German in 1929 by Insel Verlag in Leipzig, compiled by Kappus three years after Rilke's death.

Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet, born 4 December 1875 in Prague and died 29 December 1926 in Switzerland; his best-known works include Duino Elegies, Sonnets to Orpheus and The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge.
The Academy of American Poets biography gives Rilke's dates as 1875-1926 (born 4 December 1875 in Prague, died 29 December 1926 in Switzerland) and lists Letters to a Young Poet among his prose.
A site search of Quote Investigator for "live the questions" returns no article investigating this Rilke quotation.
